Born in Georgia, this Red Army officer and engineer was the eldest son of a Bolshevik revolutionary who became head of the Soviet Union — who is he?
Yakov Dzhugashvili: Red Army officer and Joseph Stalin's son (1907–1943)
Founder of the Pakistan People's Party, this barrister-statesman served as both president and prime minister of Pakistan before his 1977 overthrow and 1979 execution — who was he?
Zulfikar Ali Bhutto: 4th President and 9th Prime Minister of Pakistan (1928–1979)
Which one below was born first?
Mikhail Lomonosov (born 1711) is the earliest of the four. One of the founders of modern geology, Lomonosov was also a poet and influenced the formation of the modern Russian literary language.
Which of these people was born first?
Zhuge Liang (born 181) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four dates back furthest?
Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four began earliest?
Pascal (programming language) (founded 1970) is the earliest of the four. It is named after French mathematician, philosopher and physicist Blaise Pascal.
Pick the astronomer from these four.
Galileo Galilei is an astronomer. Galileo has been called the father of observational astronomy, modern-era classical physics, the scientific method, and modern science.
Which one below is best known as a mathematician?
Blaise Pascal is a mathematician. Blaise Pascal (19 June 1623 – 19 August 1662) was a French mathematician, physicist, inventor, philosopher, and Catholic writer.
What is the atomic number of Unbinilium?
Unbinilium, also known as eka-radium or element 120, is a hypothetical chemical element; it has symbol Ubn and atomic number 120.
What is the atomic number of Arsenic?
Arsenic is a chemical element; it has the symbol As and atomic number 33.
In what year did Ted Kaczynski die?
Ted Kaczynski: The FBI used the case identifier UNABOM (University and Airline Bombing) before his identity was known, resulting in the media naming him the "Unabomber".
In what year was Angelman syndrome discovered?
Angelman syndrome (AS) is a rare genetic disorder that affects approximately 1 in 15,000 individuals.

Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-19: Russian Aircraft Corporation MiG. The Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-19 (Russian: Микоян и Гуревич МиГ-19; NATO reporting name: Farmer) is a Soviet second generation, single-seat, twinjet fighter aircraft.
Yakovlev MC-21: United Aircraft Corporation. The aircraft made its maiden flight on 28 May 2017 from Irkutsk.
Which country is McDonnell Douglas F-15E Strike Eagle from?

McDonnell Douglas F-15E Strike Eagle: United States. The McDonnell Douglas (now Boeing) F-15E Strike Eagle is an American all-weather multirole strike fighter derived from the McDonnell Douglas F-15 Eagle.
Who is credited with discovering Nihonium?
Nihonium: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research. Nihonium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Nh and atomic number 113.
Who is credited with discovering Mass–energy equivalence?
Mass–energy equivalence: Albert Einstein. In physics, mass–energy equivalence is the relationship between mass and energy in a system's rest frame.
Who is credited with discovering Plesiosaurus?
Plesiosaurus: Mary Anning. It is known by nearly complete skeletons from the Lias of England.
Sometimes called ajowan caraway or carom, this annual herb in the carrot family produces a seed-like fruit often confused with lovage — what is it?
Ajwain (Trachyspermum ammi) - also known as ajowan caraway, thymol seeds, bishop's weed, or carom - is an annual herb in the family Apiaceae.

With more than 140 species spread across 16 genera in oceans worldwide, these small forage fish are usually classified as oily fish, and a few South American species live only in fresh water — name this fish?
Anchovy are small, common forage fish of the family Engraulidae.

Which plant family of about 181 genera and 2,600 species, nearly all found in the tropics, includes climbers, shrubs, and tree-like forms with large fan- or feather-shaped fronds atop mostly unbranched stems?
Arecaceae are a family of perennial, flowering plants in the monocot order Arecales.
The only mammals capable of true sustained flight, members of this order — the second largest among mammals — fly using long digits webbed by a thin membrane. What are they?
Bat (order Chiroptera) are winged mammals, the only mammals capable of true and sustained flight.
Native to cool parts of Europe and Asia, this deciduous shrub produces small, glossy black berries especially rich in vitamin C and vulnerable to cold snaps during spring flowering — name the fruit?
Blackcurrant (Ribes nigrum), black currant or cassis is a deciduous shrub in the family Grossulariaceae grown for its edible berries.

Forced to flee Italy in 1938 under the racial laws, this experimental physicist had earlier invented an improved coincidence circuit and traveled to Eritrea to show cosmic rays arrived more strongly from the West than the East — who was he?
Bruno Rossi (13 April 1905 - 21 November 1993) was an Italian-American experimental physicist.

Honored twice by the American Psychological Association — in 1956 for scientific contributions and 1972 for professional ones — this psychologist championed a person-centered approach to therapy — who is he?
Carl Rogers (January 8, 1902 - February 4, 1987) was an American psychologist who was one of the founders of humanistic psychology and was known especially for his person-centered psychotherapy.

This compound is a yellowish-green gas above 11°C, a reddish-brown liquid when cooler, and bright orange crystals when very cold — usually handled in solution as a bleach and disinfectant. What is it?

Chlorine dioxide is a chemical compound with the formula ClO2 that exists as yellowish-green gas above 11 C (52 F), a reddish-brown liquid between 11 and 59 C (52 and 74 F), and as bright orange crystals below 59 C (74 F).
What's the scientific family name for the group of birds that includes both doves and pigeons — stout-bodied birds with small heads and no formal distinction between the two common names?
Columbidae is a bird family consisting of doves and pigeons.
This bird family, the sole one in its taxonomic order, includes roadrunners, koels, malkohas, and coucals across roughly 150 species. Name the family?
Cuckoo are birds in the family Cuculidae, the sole taxon in the order Cuculiformes.
Mother of Princess Alia, this royal later remarried a senior PLO official in 1970 after her short-lived marriage to Jordan's king ended — who is she?
Dina bint Abdul-Hamid (15 December 1929 - 21 August 2019) was a Hashemite princess and Queen of Jordan from 1955 until 1957 as the first wife of King Hussein.

This is the industrial process of converting other forms of energy into electric power, typically at power plants using electromechanical devices, before it is transmitted and distributed to end users. What is this process called?
Electricity generation is the process of generating electric power from sources of primary energy.

This genus of 700-plus flowering trees gets its name from Greek words meaning 'well covered' — a nod to the little cap fused over its stamens — and most species are native to Australia. The leafy 'gum trees' in question are which?
Eucalyptus is a genus of more than 700 species of flowering plants in the family Myrtaceae.
Found at the terminal end of the limb in many vertebrates, this weight-bearing anatomical structure enables locomotion and is typically made up of multiple bony segments — what is it?
Foot (pl.: feet) is an anatomical structure found in many vertebrates. The plural form feet is an instance of i-mutation.

Sharing the 1988 Nobel Prize, this American biochemist pioneered rational drug design — studying a drug's target rather than relying on trial and error — and her work led to AZT, the first widely used AIDS drug. Who was she?
Gertrude B. Elion (January 23, 1918 - February 21, 1999) was an American biochemist and pharmacologist, who shared the 1988 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with George H. Hitchings.
Born Herman Webster Mudgett, this con artist and killer worked his crimes around the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, earning the nickname "the Beast of Chicago" — who was he?
H. H. Holmes (May 16, 1861 - May 7, 1896), better known as Dr.

Often called the "father of the Indian nuclear programme," this theoretical physicist founded the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research and the research centre later renamed in his honour. Who was he?
Homi J. Bhabha (30 October 1909 - 24 January 1966) was an Indian nuclear theoretical physicist who is widely credited as the "father of the Indian nuclear programme".

Dubbed the 'saviour of mothers,' this 19th-century Hungarian doctor demonstrated that a simple hygiene practice could drastically cut deaths from childbed fever, decades before germ theory was widely accepted — who is he?

Ignaz Semmelweis (1 July 1818 - 13 August 1865) was a Hungarian medical doctor and scientist of German descent who was an early pioneer of antiseptic procedures and was described as the "saviour of mothers".
With brownish-grey fur and a pinkish-red face, this cold-hardy primate is known colloquially by a wintry nickname referencing the snow in its habitat — which species?
Japanese macaque (Macaca fuscata), also known as the snow monkey, is a terrestrial Old World monkey species that is native to Japan.
This Hungarian-American biochemist spent years pushing past skepticism to lay the groundwork for mRNA vaccines, winning a 2023 Nobel alongside Drew Weissman. Who is she?

Katalin Karikó (born 17 January 1955) is a Hungarian and American biochemist who specializes in ribonucleic acid (RNA)-mediated mechanisms, particularly in vitro-transcribed messenger RNA (mRNA) for protein replacement therapy.

This Hungarian-born physicist conceived the nuclear chain reaction in 1933, drafted the famous letter Einstein signed to launch the Manhattan Project, then later petitioned President Truman not to drop the bomb on civilians — who was he?

Leo Szilard (born Le Spitz; February 11, 1898 - May 30, 1964) was a Hungarian-born American physicist, biologist and inventor who made numerous important discoveries in nuclear physics and the biological sciences.
Born in Winnipeg and trained at King's College London, this physicist and chemist joined the Manhattan Project in 1942 to conduct experiments with uranium — who is he?
Louis Slotin (1 December 1910 - 30 May 1946) was a Canadian physicist and chemist who took part in the Manhattan Project.
He helped uncover the Antarctic ozone hole and shared a 1995 Nobel for exposing the danger CFCs pose to the ozone layer — which Mexican chemist?
Mario Molina (19 March 1943 - 7 October 2020) was a Mexican physical chemist.
This medical condition is diagnosed when the erect length of the affected organ measures at least two and a half standard deviations below the average size for age — what condition is it?
Micropenis is an unusually small penis.
Named for the strong odor males emit during rut to attract mates, this thick-coated Arctic hoofed mammal is called 'the bearded one' in Inuktitut — what's the species?
Muskox (Ovibos moschatus) is a hoofed mammal of the family Bovidae.
A highly corrosive mineral compound with the formula HNO3, this strong inorganic acid is colorless but yellows over time as it decomposes. What is this acid?
Nitric acid is an inorganic compound with the formula HNO3. The compound is colorless, but samples tend to acquire a yellow cast over time due to decomposition into oxides of nitrogen.
Usually caused by bacteria and sometimes requiring amputation in severe cases, this infectious inflammation of bone can be acute or chronic — which condition?
Osteomyelitis (OM) is the infectious inflammation of bone. It may be acute or chronic and can be classified as hematogenous or non-hematogenous.
Recognized by a long beak and an enormous throat pouch used to drain water from scooped-up prey before swallowing, these large water birds come in eight living species worldwide — which birds?
Pelican (genus Pelecanus) are a genus of large water birds that make up the family Pelecanidae.
What small, tailless, round-bodied mountain mammal — a close relative of the rabbit with short rounded ears — includes a large-eared Himalayan species that lives above 6,000 meters?
Pika is a small, mountain-dwelling mammal native to Asia and North America.

Caused by the loss of function of specific genes on chromosome 15, this rare genetic disorder leads to weak muscles and poor feeding in infancy, then constant hunger and risk of obesity in childhood — what's it called?

Prader–Willi syndrome (PWS) is a rare genetic disorder caused by a loss of function of specific genes on chromosome 15. A similar mechanism occurs in Angelman syndrome, except the defective chromosome 15 is from the mother, or two copies are from the father.
This white, odorless nitroamine explosive, widely used since World War II, is the explosive agent inside C-4 plastic explosive — what is it called?
RDX (Research Department Explosive or Royal Demolition Explosive), or hexogen, also known by other names, is an organic compound with the formula (CH2N2O2)3.
Made by steaming dehusked oat groats before flattening them under heavy rollers and lightly toasting them, this whole-grain food becomes porridge when cooked — which product?
Rolled oats are a type of lightly processed whole-grain food.

After early attempts at family-friendly Christian video games found little success, this American developer switched to horror in 2014 and created a hit franchise about animatronic mascots that come alive at night — who is he?

Scott Cawthon (born June 4, 1978) is an American video game developer, writer, and producer best known for creating Five Nights at Freddy's, a series of horror video games which expanded into a media franchise.
Some of these organisms merge single cells into visible fruiting bodies via chemical signals called acrasins, aiding in the decay of vegetation — what group is this?
Slime mold (British) are a variety of small or microscopic organisms in different groups.
An English dyer and astronomer, this man's 1729 experiments were the first to systematically show that electricity could travel through metals and appear on the surface of insulators — who was he?
Stephen Gray (scientist) (December 1666 - February 1736) was an English dyer and astronomer who was the first to systematically experiment with electrical conduction.

A carnivorous marsupial formerly found across mainland Australia but now confined to Tasmania, this animal became the world's largest carnivorous marsupial after the thylacine's extinction in 1936. What is this fierce creature?
Tasmanian devil (Sarcophilus harrisii; palawa kani: purinina) is a carnivorous marsupial of the family Dasyuridae.
Found in nature only as an oxide and locked in minerals like rutile and ilmenite, this strong, silvery element bears the name of mythological giants — what is it?
Titanium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ti and atomic number 22.

An oily, amber-colored liquid that's extremely non-volatile and therefore lingers in the environment, this organophosphorus compound was developed for chemical warfare and is lethal in doses of just tens of milligrams — which chemical agent?
VX (nerve agent) is an extremely toxic synthetic chemical compound in the organophosphorus class, specifically, a thiophosphonate.
The first-ever recipient of the Nobel Prize in Physics, this German scientist discovered a form of electromagnetic radiation named after him in some languages — who was he?

Wilhelm Röntgen (27 March 1845 - 10 February 1923) was a German experimental physicist who produced and detected electromagnetic radiation in a wavelength range known as X-rays (known as Rntgen rays in many languages).
Also called the belly, this body region sits between the chest and pelvis and is known as the metasoma in arthropods — which body part?
Abdomen: Part of the body between the chest and pelvis. The area occupied by the abdomen is called the abdominal cavity.

Now built by Leonardo but originally developed jointly by an Italian and an American helicopter maker, this 15-seat medium twin-engine helicopter serves VIP transport, firefighting, and search-and-rescue roles — which aircraft?
De Havilland Canada DHC-6 Twin Otter
AgustaWestland AW139: Twin-engined, medium-lift helicopter manufactured by Leonardo.

Believed to be an autoimmune attack on the immune privilege of hair follicles, this condition typically leaves a few coin-sized bald spots — and in rare cases takes every hair on the body. What's it called?
Alopecia areata: Medical condition. Alopecia areata (AA), also known as spot baldness, is a condition in which hair is lost from some or all areas of the body.
This English mathematician earned a knighthood and the Abel Prize for proving Fermat's Last Theorem, a problem that fascinated him since childhood in Nigeria. Who is he?
Andrew Wiles: British mathematician who proved Fermat's Last Theorem.

Latin for 'worm-shaped,' this finger-like, blind-ended tube branches off the cecum and, though long considered vestigial, may actually serve as a reservoir for beneficial gut bacteria. What structure is this?
Appendix (anatomy): Tube attached to the intestine.
Known medically as tinea pedis, this common fungal infection often begins between the toes and spreads in places like swimming pools and locker rooms — what is it?
Athlete's foot: Skin infection caused by fungus.

Developed in the 18th century by an English clergyman and, independently, by Pierre-Simon Laplace, this rule lets you flip a conditional probability — say, finding the odds a patient is sick given a positive test. What is it?
Bayes' theorem: Mathematical rule for inverting probabilities.
Prized for the rainbow, iridescent crust that forms when it oxidizes under heat, which brittle, silvery element is only 86 percent as dense as lead?
Bismuth: Chemical element with atomic number 83 (Bi)
Also nicknamed 'starflower,' this Mediterranean annual herb yields seed oil despite containing small amounts of toxic alkaloids — which plant?
Borage: Species of flowering plant in the family Boraginaceae.
Caused by heat, electricity, chemicals, friction, or radiation — and most often the result of scalding at home — what type of skin injury is classified from first- to higher-degree severity?
Burn: Injury to flesh or skin, often caused by excessive heat.
Nicknamed for its heart-shaped seed pods, this mustard-family weed is considered protocarnivorous because its seeds ooze a mucilage that traps nematodes — which species?
Capsella bursa-pastoris: Species of flowering plant in the mustard family.
Which biological process oxidizes nutrients using an electron acceptor such as oxygen to generate ATP, the universal energy currency of life?
Cellular respiration: Process of releasing energy from nutrients using inorganic electron acceptors.

The second-lightest halogen, this yellow-green gas is so reactive it has the highest electron affinity of any element and once fascinated medieval alchemists heating chloride salts — which element is it?
Chlorine: Chemical element with atomic number 17 (Cl)
This process turns blood from liquid to gel through platelet activation and fibrin formation, beginning almost instantly after a vessel is injured — what's the clotting process called?
Coagulation: Process of formation of blood clots. Coagulation, also known as clotting, is the process by which blood changes from a liquid to a gel forming a blood clot.

This physical law holds that within an isolated system, nothing is created or destroyed — only transformed, as when a stick of dynamite converts stored chemical potential into heat, sound, and motion — what law is it?
Conservation of energy: Law of physics and chemistry.
This species includes honeydew, cantaloupe, and Casaba varieties, and traveled along ancient caravan routes long before its exact origin in the Levant or Egypt was ever confirmed — what fruit is it?
Cucumis melo: Species of plant. Cucumis melo, also known as melon or true melon, is a species of Cucumis that has been developed into many cultivated varieties.
Striking 48 to 72 hours after a heavy drinker's last drink, this potentially fatal condition brings hallucinations, seizures nicknamed 'rum fits,' and dangerously high body temperature — what is it?
Delirium tremens: Rapid onset of confusion caused by alcohol withdrawal.
Bred in Córdoba in the early 1900s to hunt wild boar and puma, this large mastiff-type breed's ancestry includes an extinct local fighting dog and a Bull Terrier — which breed is it?
Dogo Argentino: Argentine breed of dog. It was bred in the early twentieth century in Córdoba in central Argentina, primarily for hunting large game such as peccaries, wild boar, and pumas.
One of the Hungarian émigré scientists nicknamed the "Martians," he extended Fermi's theory of beta decay and is colloquially called the father of the hydrogen bomb — who was he?

Dubbed a 'living fossil' and commonly known as horsetail, this spore-reproducing plant genus once included 30-meter-tall trees in Carboniferous forests, its node-spacing pattern said to have inspired the invention of logarithms — which genus?

With a rich chestnut crown and a bold black patch on each white cheek, this small Old World songbird nests in cavities, walls, or abandoned magpie nests, and lays five or six eggs that hatch in under two weeks — which bird?
Eurasian tree sparrow: Species of bird. The sexes have similar plumage, and young birds are duller versions of the adult.
Marketed under brand names like Allegra, this second-generation antihistamine treats allergy symptoms without crossing the blood-brain barrier the way older drugs do — what medication is it?
Fexofenadine: Antihistamine medication. Fexofenadine is an antihistamine medication used in the treatment of allergy symptoms such as allergic rhinitis and urticaria.
Dead at just 26, this British thinker had already reshaped philosophy, mathematics and economics — and as an undergraduate translated Wittgenstein's 'Tractatus' into English; who was he?
Frank P. Ramsey: British philosopher, mathematician and economist (1903–1930)
This scientific field measures Earth's precise shape, gravity, and orientation in space, underpinning satellite positioning systems and global mapping — which discipline?
Geodesy: Science of measuring the shape, orientation, and gravity of Earth.
This type of organ produces an organism's sex hormones and gametes — testicles in males, ovaries in females — what is it called?
Gonad: Gland that produces sex cells.
This standard markup language structures web documents using elements delineated by tags, often paired with CSS and JavaScript — what is it?
HTML: Markup language for documents. Hypertext Markup Language (HTML) is the standard markup language for documents designed to be displayed in a web browser.
This natural anticoagulant boosts the activity of antithrombin and is used to prevent clotting during dialysis and in blood test tubes — what medication is it?
Heparin: Anticoagulant. Heparin, also known as unfractionated heparin (UFH), is a medication and naturally occurring glycosaminoglycan.

This American physicist dared to drop the wave-function-collapse postulate, proposing a 'relative state' theory that became the basis of the many-worlds interpretation — largely ignored until quantum decoherence vindicated him. Who is he?

Extracted from a Central African plant sacred to Gabon's Bwiti tradition, this hallucinogenic alkaloid was once marketed in Europe as a stimulant before being studied for other therapeutic uses — what is it?
Ibogaine: Psychoactive substance found in plants in the family Apocynaceae.

A theoretical physicist who studied under Max Born earned a chemistry degree from Harvard before pivoting to nuclear physics — and later oversaw the first atomic weapons during WWII. Who is this pivotal figure in physics history?
J. Robert Oppenheimer: American theoretical physicist (1904–1967)
In a landmark 1913 Columbia University address, this American psychologist championed behaviorism and later became known for the unsettling 'Little Albert' experiment — who is he?
Nicknamed 'The Professor' on The Chase, this record-breaking contestant won 74 consecutive games on a legendary quiz show in 2004 before eventually becoming its host — who is he?
Ken Jennings: American game show host (born 1974)
This reddish-brown, bitter tincture dissolved opium poppy extract in alcohol and was once sold without a prescription as a cough and pain remedy — what is it?
Laudanum: Tincture of opium. Laudanum is a tincture of opium containing approximately 10% powdered opium by weight (the equivalent of 1% morphine).
Native to the Indo-Pacific, this venomous aquarium favorite sports red-and-black banded warning colors and ostentatious spiny fins, and has become an invasive nightmare in the Caribbean — what is it?
This flowering legume genus boasts over 199 species and has become such a successful invasive spreader in Iceland that it's now considered an ecological problem — which genus?
Dubbed "sea locusts" by the ancient Assyrians and "prawn killers" by others, these burrow-dwelling crustaceans are among the most important predators of shallow tropical seas. What are they?
Mantis shrimp: Order of crustaceans. Mantis shrimp are carnivorous marine crustaceans of the order Stomatopoda (from Ancient Greek στόμα (stóma) 'mouth' and πούς (poús) 'foot').
Made up of the dura, arachnoid, and pia mater, these three protective membranes shield the brain and spinal cord while containing cerebrospinal fluid — what are they called?
Meninges: Three membranes protecting the brain. In anatomy, the meninges (sing. meninx; from Ancient Greek μῆνινξ (mêninx) 'membrane') are protective membranes that cover the brain and spinal cord.

An advanced modification of its Korean War-era predecessor, this Soviet transonic fighter — NATO reporting name 'Fresco' — was license-built in China and Poland, and remains in North Korean service today — which jet?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-17: Soviet jet fighter aircraft family.
Nicknamed noni, this pungent-smelling fruit tree in the coffee family was spread across the Pacific by Polynesian sailors and is now used mainly in traditional medicine and juices — which plant?
Morinda citrifolia: Species of plant. It is commonly known as noni or Indian mulberry, among many other names.
Made of two fused benzene rings, this pungent white crystalline compound is the main ingredient in traditional mothballs — what is it?
Naphthalene: Chemical compound. It is a white crystalline solid with a characteristic odor that is detectable at concentrations as low as 0.08 ppm.
Unlike its more predictably spreading cousin, this group of blood cancers can appear in multiple parts of the body at once and cause enlarged lymph nodes, fevers, and night sweats — which condition?
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma: Type of cancer of lymph nodes.
In this learning process, voluntary behaviors are shaped by their consequences — strengthened by reinforcement, weakened by punishment or extinction. What is it called?
Operant conditioning: Type of associative learning process for behavioral modification.
This B vitamin's name comes from the Greek for "from everywhere," since it turns up in nearly all foods, and animals need it to build coenzyme A — what is it?
This term describes a short chain of amino acids joined by a particular kind of bond; string together enough of them (10,000 daltons or more) and you get a protein instead — what is it?
Peptide: Short chains of 2–50 amino acids.
This healthcare profession uses patient education and hands-on interventions to prevent, treat, and restore mobility, with specialties from sports medicine to pediatrics — which field?
Physical therapy: Profession that helps a disabled person function in everyday life.
Built from many linked simple sugars and including starch, glycogen, and cellulose among its examples, this class of carbohydrate is the most abundant in our food — what is it called?
Polysaccharide: Long carbohydrate polymers such as starch, glycogen, cellulose, and chitin.
This thorny European shrub's tart fruit gives sloe gin its name in Britain, while its wood becomes the classic Irish walking stick — what is it?
Prunus spinosa: Species of flowering plant in the rose family.
Domesticated in Asia, this crunchy root vegetable in the mustard family owes its peppery bite to compounds like glucosinolate — what vegetable is it?
Radish: Root vegetable of the Brassicaceae family. The radish (Raphanus sativus or Raphanus raphanistrum subsp. sativus) is a flowering plant in the mustard family, Brassicaceae.

Grown for its fleshy, edible stalks since before the 18th century in Europe and Scandinavia, this plant's broad triangular leaves are actually poisonous due to their high oxalic acid content. What is it?
Rhubarb: Species of herbaceous perennial plant with fleshy, sour edible stalks.
First identified in November 2002 and traced through civets to horseshoe bats in Yunnan, this viral respiratory disease had an 11% fatality rate before its outbreak ended in 2003 — which disease?
Creator of a satirical comic strip about corporate cubicle life, this cartoonist also wrote the pandeistic novella 'God's Debris' — who is he?
Scott Adams: American cartoonist and author (1957–2026)
In this inherited blood disorder, faulty haemoglobin warps red cells into a rigid crescent shape that can't bend through capillaries, causing painful blockages — what is it?
Also nicknamed 'sour dock,' this perennial herb native to Eurasia is often eaten as a tangy leaf vegetable in grassland habitats — which plant?
Sorrel: Flowering plant in the family Polygonaceae.
In this eye disorder, the two eyes fail to align properly on the same object, which can cause a lazy eye and lost depth perception if it persists through much of childhood. What condition is it?
Strabismus: Eyes not aligning when looking at something.
Named by Linnaeus in 1753 but called cempōhualxōchitl by the Nahua long before, this genus of Mexican-native flowers is commonly known as marigolds — what's the genus?
A cousin of caffeine found in trace amounts in tea, coffee, and chocolate, which methylxanthine drug is used to treat asthma and COPD by blocking adenosine receptors?
Theophylline: Drug used to treat respiratory diseases.
This field of geoscience studies the shape of land surfaces — not just elevation, but roads, boundaries, and buildings too, as shown on USGS terrain maps — what is it called?
Topography: Study of the forms of land surfaces in earth.

This late Cretaceous carnivore, whose scientific name pairs a word for 'tyrant' with the Latin for 'king,' roamed western North America right up until the mass extinction 66 million years ago — which iconic predator is it?
Tyrannosaurus: Genus of Late Cretaceous theropod.
Despite a scientific name meaning 'sand burrower,' this snake actually prefers rocky terrain and is considered Europe's most dangerous viper thanks to fangs up to 13mm long — which species?
Vipera ammodytes: Species of snake. It is reputed to be the most dangerous of the European vipers due to its large size, long fangs (up to 13 mm) and high venom toxicity.
In 1879 at the University of Leipzig, this German scholar founded the first formal psychology laboratory, earning him the title 'father of experimental psychology' — who is he?
Wilhelm Wundt: German founder of psychology (1832–1920)
Known on the street as flakka or gravel, this synthetic stimulant of the cathinone class was developed in the 1960s and later sold as a designer drug — what is it?
The symbol for iridium is Ir. Iridium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Ir and atomic number 77.
